title: Moroccan grammar
variety: Moroccan Arabic (Darija), as spoken in Casablanca and Rabat
about: Only what is different from Standard Arabic, for someone who has done the Arabic grammar course: the sounds, the dropped endings, the everyday verb forms (ka-, ghādi), saying no, want, can and must, “there is”, “mine” with dyāl, rāh and yāk, the numbers and linking your ideas. Everything that works as in Standard Arabic is left out. Every example is everyday Darija as spoken in Casablanca and Rabat, with vowel marks to show how it is said (Darija is usually written without them) and a reading in Latin letters: ə is a short “uh”, gh a French r, ʿ the Arabic ع.

lessons.title: Sound like a Moroccan
lessons.summary: The regular changes that turn Standard words you know into Darija: “he wrote” is ktəb, “three” is tlāta, “this” is hād.
lessons.topic: short vowels dropped, {{ث ذ ظ|th dh ẓ}} as t, d, ḍ, the hamza dropped, {{ج|j}} as in French “jour”

goal.tr: He has just come from work.

blocks.p: Moroccan Arabic, **Darija**, is the everyday Arabic of Morocco. Many of its words are the Standard words you already know, **said differently**, and the biggest difference is speed: Darija drops most short vowels, so words start and end with groups of consonants. Learn the few regular changes below and hundreds of words you know will come back to you.

blocks.means: the everyday spoken Arabic of a region (Moroccan, Levantine, Egyptian, Gulf), as opposed to Modern Standard Arabic, the written standard every Arab learns at school.

table: short vowels drop; what is left is a short ə

blocks.p: {{ج|j}} is said like the s in “pleasure” (j in French “jour”), and {{ق|q}} stays q in the cities, while some everyday words have g, written {{ڭ|g}}: {{ڭَاعْ|gāʿ}} “all”, {{ڭَالْ|gāl}} “he said” (many people say {{قَالْ|qāl}}). The ending {{ة|a}} is said -a: {{الْخْدْمَة|l-khədma}} “work”.

ex.tr: He read the newspaper and left.

blocks.tip: Darija is written in Arabic letters without vowel marks, the way you read it on a phone or in the basics course. The marks in this course are there only to show you how it is said.

mistakes.why: Darija drops the short vowels: {{كْتَبْ|ktəb}}. With all three vowels it sounds like reading the news.
{{ث|th}} is said t in everyday words, and Darija writes it {{ت|t}}.

practice.q: How do you say {{هَذَا|hādhā}} “this” in Darija?

practice.why: The hamza goes: {{جَا|ja}}. In the same way {{قَرَأَ|qaraʔa}} is {{قْرَا|qra}}.

practice.q: How do you say “he wrote” in Darija?
Your turn: say a short sentence with a word that changed its {{ث|th}} or lost its hamza.

answers.tr: He has just come.
I have three books.

lessons.title: Drop the endings: two of a thing, and plurals
lessons.summary: No case endings at all, “two” is jūj with a plural, and one plural ending -īn for every adjective.
lessons.topic: no {{ـُ ـَ ـِ|u a i}} endings or tanwin, {{جُوجْ|jūj}} + plural instead of the dual, adjectives in {{ـِينْ|-īn}}

blocks.p: Darija has **no case endings**: no -u, -a or -i at the end of a word, no tanwin (-un, -an, -in). A word sounds the same as subject, object or after a preposition: {{الدَّارْ|d-dār}} “the house”, {{فْالدَّارْ|f-d-dār}} “in the house”. A few fixed words keep -an from Standard: {{شُكْرًا|shukran}} “thank you”, {{مَثَلًا|mathalan}} “for example”.

**The dual is gone** for most things. “Two” is {{جُوجْ|jūj}}, followed by the plural, usually with {{دْ|d}} or {{دْيَالْ|dyāl}} (“of”): {{جُوجْ دْ الدّْرَارِي|jūj d d-drāri}} “two children”. Only words for time and amounts keep a dual in {{ـِينْ|-īn}} or {{ـَايْنْ|-āyn}}: {{يُومَايْنْ|yumāyn}} “two days”, {{عَامَايْنْ|ʿāmāyn}} “two years”, {{سَاعْتَيْنْ|sāʿtayn}} “two hours”, {{مَرْتَيْنْ|mərtayn}} “twice”.

**One plural for adjectives.** An adjective is masculine, feminine ({{ـَة|-a}}) or plural ({{ـِينْ|-īn}}), and the plural is the same for men and women: {{الدّْرَارِي مْزْيَانِينْ|d-drāri mzyānīn}} “the children are good”, {{الْبْنَاتْ مْزْيَانِينْ|l-bnāt mzyānīn}} “the girls are good”. Verbs have no feminine plural either.

ex.tr: We ate in a nice restaurant.
I stayed two days in Marrakech.

blocks.tip: {{وَاحْدْ|wāḥəd}} “one” before a noun with the article means “a, a certain”: {{وَاحْدْ الرَّاجْلْ|wāḥəd r-rājəl}} “a man”. Darija uses it where English says “a”.

mistakes.why: Only time words keep a dual. “Two” is {{جُوجْ|jūj}} + {{دْ|d}} + the plural.
Adjectives have one plural in {{ـِينْ|-īn}}, for women too.

practice.q: Your turn: say how many brothers, sisters or friends you have, with {{جُوجْ|jūj}} or another number.

answers.tr: I have two brothers.
I have one sister.

lessons.title: Say I, you, he, she: pronouns and “my, his, her”
lessons.summary: The Darija pronouns (āna, nta, nti, ḥna…) and the endings for “my, your, his”: dāri “my house”, dāru “his house”.
lessons.topic: {{أَنَا نْتَا نْتِي هُوَ هِيَ حْنَا نْتُومَا هُومَا|āna nta nti huwa hiya ḥna ntūma hūma}}, endings {{ـِي ـكْ ـُو ـهَا ـنَا ـكُمْ ـهُمْ|-i -k -u -ha -na -kum -hum}}

blocks.p: Darija's pronouns are the Standard ones, shortened, with no dual and no feminine plural. **“You” is nta to a man and nti to a woman**, but the ending for “your” is the same for both: {{ـكْ|-k}}. And **“his” is -u**, not -hu: {{دَارُو|dāru}} “his house”.

After a vowel “my” is {{ـيَا|-ya}} and “his” is {{ـهْ|-h}}: {{لِيَّا|liyya}} “to me”, {{عْلِيهْ|ʿlīh}} “on him”. The same endings go on verbs for “me, you, him”: {{شَافْنِي|shāfni}} “he saw me”, {{شَافُو|shāfu}} “he saw him”.

ex.tr: Her husband works in an office.
He saw me and didn't talk to me.

blocks.tip: Many people say {{نْتَا|nta}} to a woman too, and in the north you will hear {{نْتِينَا|ntīna}} and {{نْتُومَا|ntūma}} for “you”. The endings never change.

mistakes.why: “His” is {{ـُو|-u}} after a consonant: {{دَارُو|dāru}}.
Darija drops the first vowel: {{نْتَا|nta}}.

practice.why: “His” is {{ـُو|-u}} after a consonant: {{سَارُوتُو|sārūtu}}. {{سَارُوتْهَا|sārūtha}} is “her key”.

practice.q: At a café: choose your replies.
Your turn: say where you and someone in your family are from.

answers.t: أَنَا مْنْ لُنْدُنْ وْ مْرَاتِي مْنْ فَاسْ.
answers.r: āna mən lundun u mrāti mən fās.
answers.tr: I'm from London and my wife is from Fes.
We're from Casablanca.

lessons.title: Point at things: this, that, these
lessons.summary: hād before any noun (“this”), dāk, dīk, dūk for “that, those”, and hādshi, dākshi for “this, that (stuff)”.
lessons.topic: {{هَادْ|hād}} + noun, {{هَادَا هَادِي هَادُو|hāda hādi hādu}}, {{دَاكْ دِيكْ دُوكْ|dāk dīk dūk}}, {{هَادْشِي دَاكْشِي|hādshi dākshi}}

blocks.p: **“This” before a noun is hād, for everything**: a man, a woman, many people. The noun keeps its article: {{هَادْ الرَّاجْلْ|hād r-rājəl}} “this man”, {{هَادْ الدَّارْ|hād d-dār}} “this house”, {{هَادْ النَّاسْ|hād n-nās}} “these people”.

**Alone**, as “this one”, it agrees: {{هَادَا|hāda}} (masculine), {{هَادِي|hādi}} (feminine), {{هَادُو|hādu}} (plural). **“That”** is {{دَاكْ|dāk}}, {{دِيكْ|dīk}}, {{دُوكْ|dūk}}, before a noun too: {{دِيكْ الْبْنْتْ|dīk l-bənt}} “that girl”. With {{هَا|hā}} in front they point harder: {{هَادَاكْ|hādāk}} “that one there”.

**“This stuff, that thing”**: {{هَادْشِي|hādshi}} and {{دَاكْشِي|dākshi}} (with {{شِي|shi}}, “thing”) stand for an idea or things in general: {{هَادْشِي زْوِينْ|hādshi zwīn}} “this is nice”, {{دَاكْشِي اللِّي بْغِيتْ|dākshi lli bghīt}} “that's what I wanted”.

ex.tr: This is my sister, and this is my brother.
I want that one, not this one.

mistakes.why: Before a noun, “this” is {{هَادْ|hād}} for every noun. {{هَادِي|hādi}} alone means “this one (feminine)”.
{{ذ|dh}} is said d, and before a noun the word is short: {{هَادْ|hād}}.

practice.q: Pointing at a woman: “This is my sister.”

practice.why: {{دَاكْشِي|dākshi}} is “that stuff, that”: an idea or things in general.

practice.q: How do you say “This is nice” (about a thing in general)?
Your turn: point at something near you and say something about it with {{هَادْ|hād}}.

answers.tr: This coffee is cold.
This book is nice.

lessons.title: Ask what, who, where, when, why and how
lessons.summary: Darija's own question words (shnu, shkūn, fīn, fūqāsh, ʿlāsh, kīfāsh, shḥāl) and wāsh for yes-or-no questions.
lessons.topic: {{شْنُو آشْ شْكُونْ فِينْ مْنِينْ فُوقَاشْ عْلَاشْ كِيفَاشْ شْحَالْ أَشْمَنْ|shnu āsh shkūn fīn mnīn fūqāsh ʿlāsh kīfāsh shḥāl ashmən}}, {{وَاشْ|wāsh}}

blocks.p: Almost every question word is new. Most are built from Standard pieces you will recognise once you see them: {{عْلَاشْ|ʿlāsh}} is “on what” ({{عْلَى|ʿla}} + {{آشْ|āsh}}), {{كِيفَاشْ|kīfāsh}} is “how what”. The question word comes **first**, and the rest of the sentence is an ordinary statement.

table: {{شْنُو كَتْدِيرْ؟|shnu katdīr?}} What are you doing?
{{فِينْ سَاكْنْ؟|fīn sākən?}} Where do you live?
{{مْنِينْ نْتَا؟|mnīn nta?}} Where are you from?
{{فُوقَاشْ جَايْ؟|fūqāsh jāy?}} When are you coming?
{{عْلَاشْ مْقَلّْقْ؟|ʿlāsh mqəlləq?}} Why are you upset?
{{شْحَالْ هَادِي؟|shḥāl hādi?}} How much is this?

blocks.p: **Yes-or-no questions** start with {{وَاشْ|wāsh}}, which turns a statement into a question, like “do” or “is” in English: {{وَاشْ نْتَا مْغْرْبِي؟|wāsh nta məghribi?}} “Are you Moroccan?” In speech you can also just raise your voice at the end.

ex.tr: What do you want to eat?
When is the match going to start?
How many children do you have?

mistakes.why: “What” is {{شْنُو|shnu}} (or {{آشْ|āsh}}); {{مَاذَا|mādhā}} is Standard only.
Yes-or-no questions start with {{وَاشْ|wāsh}}, never {{هَلْ|hal}}.

practice.q: At the market: choose your replies.
How do you ask “When are you coming?”
Your turn: ask a new Moroccan friend three questions.

answers.t: شْنُو سْمِيتْكْ؟ مْنِينْ نْتَا؟ فِينْ سَاكْنْ؟
answers.r: shnu smītək? mnīn nta? fīn sākən?
answers.tr: What's your name? Where are you from? Where do you live?
Are you from Casablanca?

lessons.title: Say what you do: the ka- present
lessons.summary: kanktəb “I write”, katktəb “you write”: ka- in front of the present for what you do or are doing, and n- for “I”.
lessons.topic: {{كَـ|ka-}} + the present; {{نْـ|n-}} for “I” and {{نْـ…ـُو|n-…-u}} for “we”; the bare present after {{بْغِيتْ|bghīt}} and {{بَاشْ|bāsh}}

blocks.p: The present has the same person prefixes as Standard, with two changes: **“I” is n-** ({{نْكْتَبْ|nktəb}}, not {{أَكْتُبُ|aktubu}}), and **“we” is n-…-u** ({{نْكْتْبُو|nkətbu}}). There is no -na ending and no feminine plural.

To say what you **do or are doing**, put {{كَـ|ka-}} in front: {{كَنْكْتَبْ|kanktəb}} “I write, I'm writing”. In Marrakech and the north you also hear {{تَـ|ta-}}: {{تَنْكْتَبْ|tanktəb}}. Without {{كَـ|ka-}}, the bare present is for “to do”, after {{بْغِيتْ|bghīt}} “I want”, {{بَاشْ|bāsh}} “so that”, {{خَاصّْنِي|khāṣṣni}} “I must”: {{بْغِيتْ نْكْتَبْ|bghīt nktəb}} “I want to write”.

ex.tr: What are you doing now? (to a woman)
I want to watch the match.

blocks.tip: Darija writes {{كَـ|ka-}} joined to the verb, and sometimes with a long a: {{كَانْكْتَبْ|kanktəb}}, {{كَايْكْتَبْ|kayktəb}}. It is the same word.

mistakes.why: “I” is {{نْـ|n-}} in Darija: {{كَنْكْتَبْ|kanktəb}}.

mistakes.tr: I want to watch the match.
mistakes.why: After “want”, the verb is the bare present, without {{كَـ|ka-}}.

practice.tr: I want to watch the match.

practice.q: How do you ask a woman “What are you doing now?”
Your turn: say two things you do every day.

answers.tr: I wake up early and drink coffee.
I work and study Darija.

lessons.title: Talk about the future: ghādi
lessons.summary: ghādi (or gha-) before the bare present for what you will do: ghādi nmshi “I'm going to go”.

goal.tr: I'm going to the beach tomorrow.

blocks.p: Darija has no {{سَـ|sa-}} or {{سَوْفَ|sawfa}}. For the future, put {{غَادِي|ghādi}} (literally “going”) before the **bare present**, the one without {{كَـ|ka-}}: {{غَادِي نْكْتَبْ|ghādi nktəb}} “I'll write, I'm going to write”.

{{غَادِي|ghādi}} is an adjective, so it can agree with the person: {{غَادْيَة|ghādya}} for a woman, {{غَادْيِينْ|ghādyīn}} for more than one. In quick speech it shrinks to {{غَا|gha-}}, joined to the verb: {{غَانْمْشِي|ghanmshi}} “I'll go”.

ex.tr: Are you going to come with us? (to a woman)
The match is going to start now.
We're going to travel to Fes.

blocks.tip: {{غَادِي|ghādi}} alone, with no verb after it, still means “going”: {{أَنَا غَادِي لْلدَّارْ|āna ghādi l-d-dār}} “I'm going home”.

mistakes.why: The future is {{غَادِي|ghādi}} + the present with {{نْـ|n-}} for “I”.
After {{غَادِي|ghādi}} the verb has no {{كَـ|ka-}}.

practice.tr: I'm going to go to the beach.

practice.q: A woman says “I'm going to come”:
practice.why: {{غَادِي|ghādi}} agrees with her: {{غَادْيَة|ghādya}}, and the verb is bare.

practice.tr: We're going to travel to Fes.

practice.q: How do you say “I'll call you later”?
Your turn: what are you going to do this weekend?

answers.tr: I'm going to see my friends and we'll go for a walk.
I'll stay at home and sleep.

lessons.title: Tell what happened: the past
lessons.summary: The Darija past endings: ktəbt “I wrote”, ktəbti “you wrote”, ktbat “she wrote”, ktbu “they wrote”.
lessons.topic: past endings {{ـتْ ـتِي ـاتْ ـنَا ـتُو ـُو|-t -ti -at -na -tu -u}}; verbs in -a: {{بْغِيتْ|bghīt}}, {{بْغَا|bgha}}

goal.tr: Yesterday I saw your friend in the street.

blocks.p: The past has fewer endings than in Standard. **“I” and “you” are different again**: “I” is -t, and “you” is -ti for a man and a woman alike. “She” is -at, “they” is -u, and there is no dual or feminine plural.

Verbs that end in a vowel, like {{بْغَا|bgha}} “want”, {{مْشَا|msha}} “go”, {{جَا|ja}} “come”, take {{ـِيتْ|-īt}} for “I”: {{مْشِيتْ|mshīt}} “I went”. Verbs with a long ā in the middle, like {{شَافْ|shāf}}, {{جَابْ|jāb}} “bring”, {{دَارْ|dār}} “do”, shorten it: {{جْبْتْ|jəbt}} “I brought”, {{دْرْتْ|dərt}} “I did”.
**{{بْغِيتْ|bghīt}} is also “I want”, now**: Darija says what you want with the past form, {{بْغِيتْ أَتَايْ|bghīt atāy}} “I'd like some tea”.

ex.tr: I went to the hospital yesterday.
My sister came with her children.

mistakes.why: “You” is {{ـتِي|-ti}}; {{ـتْ|-t}} alone is “I”.
There is no feminine plural: women and men alike are {{ـُو|-u}}.

practice.tr: I went to the hospital yesterday.

practice.q: How do you say “I'd like some tea”?
Your turn: say two things you did yesterday.

answers.t: مْشِيتْ لْلْخْدْمَة وْ تْعْشِّيتْ مْعَا صْحَابِي.
answers.r: mshīt l-l-khədma u tʿashshīt mʿa ṣḥābi.
answers.tr: I went to work and had dinner with my friends.
I watched a film and went to bed early.

lessons.title: Say no: ma…sh and māshi
lessons.summary: ma…sh round a verb (ma bghītsh “I didn't want”), māshi before anything else (māshi mzyān “not good”), and wālu “nothing”.

goal.tr: I didn't understand, say it again please.

blocks.p: **A verb is wrapped in ma…sh**: {{مَا|ma}} before it and {{ـشْ|-sh}} at its end, after any ending: {{مَا كْتَبْتْشْ|ma ktəbtsh}} “I didn't write”, {{مَا كَنْبْغِيشْ|ma kanbghīsh}} “I don't like”, {{مَا شْفْتُوشْ|ma shəftūsh}} “I didn't see him”. Darija often writes it as one word: {{مَاكْتَبْتْشْ|maktəbtsh}}.

**Anything else takes māshi**: an adjective, a noun, a pronoun, a place, or the future: {{مَاشِي مْزْيَانْ|māshi mzyān}} “not good”, {{مَاشِي أَنَا|māshi āna}} “not me”, {{مَاشِي غَادِي نْمْشِي|māshi ghādi nmshi}} “I'm not going to go” (or {{مَا غَادِيشْ نْمْشِي|ma ghādīsh nmshi}}).

table: {{مَاشِي غَادِي نْجِي|māshi ghādi nji}} I won't come

blocks.p: With a word like {{وَالُو|wālu}} “nothing”, {{حْتَّى حَاجَة|ḥtta ḥāja}} “nothing at all” or {{حْتَّى وَاحْدْ|ḥtta wāḥəd}} “nobody”, the verb drops its {{ـشْ|-sh}}: {{مَا شْفْتْ وَالُو|ma shəft wālu}} “I saw nothing”.

ex.tr: He didn't come to work today.
I've got nothing in my wallet.

blocks.tip: “Don't!” is the same: {{مَا|ma}} + the “you” present + {{ـشْ|-sh}}: {{مَا تْمْشِيشْ|ma tmshīsh}} “don't go”, {{مَا تْخَافْشْ|ma tkhāfsh}} “don't be afraid”.

mistakes.why: Verbs are wrapped in {{مَا…شْ|ma…sh}}; {{لَا|la}} is only “no!” on its own.
An adjective takes {{مَاشِي|māshi}}, not {{مَا…شْ|ma…sh}}.

practice.tr: He didn't come to work today.

practice.q: How do you say “I didn't see anything”?
How do you say “I'm not going to come”?
Your turn: say something you don't like and something you didn't do yesterday.

answers.t: مَا كَنْبْغِيشْ الْبْرْدْ، وْ مَا خْرْجْتْشْ الْبَارْحْ.
answers.r: ma kanbghīsh l-bərd, u ma khrəjtsh l-bārəḥ.
answers.tr: I don't like the cold, and I didn't go out yesterday.
I didn't drink coffee today.

lessons.title: Say what you want, can and must
lessons.summary: bghīt “I want”, khāṣṣni “I must, I need”, kanqdər “I can”, each followed by the bare present.

goal.tr: I have to go now, I'm late.

blocks.p: **Want**: {{بْغِيتْ|bghīt}} (“I wanted”, used for “I want”) or {{بَاغِي|bāghi}} (“wanting”, {{بَاغْيَة|bāghya}} for a woman). After it, a noun, or a verb in the bare present with its own person: {{بْغِيتْ نْمْشِي|bghīt nmshi}} “I want to go”, {{بْغِيتِي تْمْشِي؟|bghīti tmshi?}} “do you want to go?”, {{بْغِيتْكْ تْجِي|bghītək tji}} “I want you to come”. {{بْغَا|bgha}} also means “to love, to like”: {{كَنْبْغِيكْ|kanbghīk}} “I love you”.

**Must, need**: {{خَاصّْ|khāṣṣ}} with the ending of the person who must: {{خَاصّْنِي|khāṣṣni}} “I must”, {{خَاصّْكْ|khāṣṣək}} “you must”, {{خَاصُّو|khāṣṣu}} “he must”, then a bare verb or a noun: {{خَاصّْنِي الْفْلُوسْ|khāṣṣni l-flūs}} “I need money”. “I don't have to” is {{مَا خَاصّْنِيشْ|ma khāṣṣnīsh}}.
**Can**: {{قْدَرْ|qdər}}, mostly in the present: {{كَنْقْدَرْ نْجِي|kanqdər nji}} “I can come”, {{مَا نْقْدَرْشْ|ma nqdərsh}} “I can't”.

ex.tr: I want to buy some trainers.
You have to pay the bill.
I (a woman) want to learn Darija.

mistakes.why: “Want” is {{بْغِيتْ|bghīt}}; {{أُرِيدُ|urīdu}} is Standard only.
After “must”, the bare present, without {{كَـ|ka-}}.

practice.why: “I must” is {{خَاصّْنِي|khāṣṣni}}, with “me” on the end.

practice.tr: Do you want to come with us?
practice.why: After “want”, the bare present with its own person: {{تْجِي|tji}}.

practice.q: A friend calls: choose your replies.

lines.tr: Do you want to come to the cinema?

practice.q: How do you say “I need money”?
Your turn: say one thing you want to do and one thing you have to do this week.

answers.t: بْغِيتْ نْمْشِي لْلْبْحَرْ، وَلَكِنْ خَاصّْنِي نْخْدْمْ.
answers.r: bghīt nmshi l-l-bḥər, walakin khāṣṣni nkhdəm.
answers.tr: I want to go to the beach, but I have to work.

answers.t: خَاصّْنِي نْتْقْدَّى وْ بْغِيتْ نْشُوفْ يْمَّا.
answers.r: khāṣṣni ntqədda u bghīt nshūf yəmma.
answers.tr: I have to do the shopping and I want to see my mum.

lessons.title: Say there is, and there isn't: kāyn and shi
lessons.summary: kāyn “there is”, makāynsh “there isn't”, and shi “some, any, a”.

blocks.p: **“There is” is kāyn**, an old participle (“being”) that agrees with what there is: {{كَايْنْ|kāyn}} (masculine, and for anything in general), {{كَايْنَة|kāyna}} (feminine), {{كَايْنِينْ|kāynīn}} (plural). **“There isn't”** wraps it in {{مَا…شْ|ma…sh}}: {{مَاكَايْنْشْ|makāynsh}}. In the past it is {{كَانْ|kān}}: {{كَانْ بْزَّافْ دْ النَّاسْ|kān bzzāf d n-nās}} “there were a lot of people”.

**{{شِي|shi}}** (from {{شَيْء|shayʔ}} “thing”) before a noun means “some, any, a”: {{شِي حَاجَة|shi ḥāja}} “something”, {{شِي وَاحْدْ|shi wāḥəd}} “someone”, {{شِي نْهَارْ|shi nhār}} “some day”. **“No … at all”** is {{حْتَّى شِي|ḥtta shi}} or {{حْتَّى|ḥtta}}: {{مَا كَايْنْ حْتَّى شِي وَاحْدْ|ma kāyn ḥtta shi wāḥəd}} “there's nobody at all”.

table: {{وَاشْ كَايْنْ شِي طُوبِيسْ؟|wāsh kāyn shi ṭūbīs?}} is there a bus?

ex.tr: There's no signal in this place.
There are a lot of people at the market.

mistakes.why: “There is” is {{كَايْنْ|kāyn}}; {{هُنَاكَ|hunāka}} is Standard only.
On its own it needs both halves: {{مَا…شْ|ma…sh}}.

practice.tr: There are a lot of people at the market.

practice.why: “No one at all” is {{حْتَّى وَاحْدْ|ḥtta wāḥəd}}, and the verb then drops its {{ـشْ|-sh}}.

practice.q: How do you say “There's no water”?
Your turn: say what there is and isn't in your street.

answers.t: فْالزّْنْقَة دْيَالِي كَايْنْ حَانُوتْ، وْ مَاكَايْنَاشْ شِي فَرْمَاسْيَانْ.
answers.r: f-z-zənqa dyāli kāyn ḥānūt, u makāynāsh shi farmasyān.
answers.tr: In my street there's a shop, and there's no pharmacy.
There are a lot of kids.

lessons.title: Say mine and yours: dyāl
lessons.summary: dyāl “of” between two nouns and with endings for “mine, yours”: ṭ-ṭonobīl dyāli “my car”.
lessons.topic: {{دْيَالْ|dyāl}}, {{دْ|d}}, {{دْيَالِي دْيَالْكْ دْيَالُو…|dyāli dyālək dyālu…}}, {{دْيَالْ شْكُونْ؟|dyāl shkūn?}}

blocks.p: Darija says “of” with **dyāl** (short {{دْ|d}}) instead of joining two nouns the Standard way. The first noun keeps its article: {{الطُّونُوبِيلْ دْيَالْ خُويَا|ṭ-ṭonobīl dyāl khūya}} “my brother's car”, {{الْبَابْ دْ الدَّارْ|l-bāb d d-dār}} “the door of the house”. {{دْيَالْ|dyāl}} never changes for masculine, feminine or plural.

With the endings you know, it means **mine, yours, his**: {{دْيَالِي|dyāli}}, {{دْيَالْكْ|dyālək}}, {{دْيَالُو|dyālu}}, {{دْيَالْهَا|dyālha}}, {{دْيَالْنَا|dyālna}}, {{دْيَالْكُمْ|dyālkum}}, {{دْيَالْهُمْ|dyālhum}}. **Things you own** usually take {{دْيَالْ|dyāl}}: {{التِّيلِيفُونْ دْيَالِي|t-tilifūn dyāli}} “my phone”. **Family and body** take the ending straight on: {{خُويَا|khūya}} “my brother”, {{رَاسِي|rāsi}} “my head”, {{دَارْنَا|dārna}} “our house”.

mistakes.why: Darija links the nouns with {{دْيَالْ|dyāl}}, and the first one keeps its article.
{{دْيَالْ|dyāl}} never changes with the noun: {{دْيَالِي|dyāli}}.

practice.q: How do you ask “Whose bag is this?”
options: {{هَادْ الصَّاكْ دْيَالْ شْكُونْ؟|hād ṣ-ṣāk dyāl shkūn?}}

practice.why: Family takes the ending straight on: {{خُويَا|khūya}}.

practice.q: How do you say “a glass of tea, please”?
Your turn: say what colour or size three of your things are, with {{دْيَالِي|dyāli}}.

answers.t: الطُّونُوبِيلْ دْيَالِي كْحْلَة، وْ الصَّاكْ دْيَالِي صْغِيرْ.
answers.r: ṭ-ṭonobīl dyāli kəḥla, u ṣ-ṣāk dyāli ṣghīr.
answers.tr: My car is black, and my bag is small.
My phone is new.

lessons.title: Point things out: rāh, yāk and wākha
lessons.summary: rāh “look, (it) is”: rāni f-d-dār “I'm at home”; yāk “right?”; wākha “OK, even if”.
lessons.topic: {{رَاهْ|rāh}} with endings ({{رَانِي رَاكْ رَاهْ رَاهَا رَاحْنَا رَاكُمْ رَاهُمْ|rāni rāk rāh rāha rāḥna rākum rāhum}}), {{يَاكْ|yāk}}, {{وَاخَّا|wākhkha}}

goal.tr: I'm on my way, wait for me.

blocks.p: **{{رَاهْ|rāh}}** points at something true right now, like “look,” or “you know,” in English, and it says who with the endings you know: {{رَانِي|rāni}} “here I am, I am”, {{رَاكْ|rāk}} “you are”, {{رَاهْ|rāh}} “he is”, {{رَاهَا|rāha}} “she is”, {{رَاحْنَا|rāḥna}}, {{رَاكُمْ|rākum}}, {{رَاهُمْ|rāhum}}. It is very common with places and states: {{رَانِي فْالدَّارْ|rāni f-d-dār}} “I'm at home”, {{رَاهْ نَاعْسْ|rāh nāʿəs}} “he's asleep”.

It also **warns or insists**: {{رَاهْ مْعَطّْلْ!|rāh mʿaṭṭəl!}} “it's late, you know!”, {{رَاكْ غَالْطْ|rāk ghālṭ}} “you're wrong”. Before a verb it gives news: {{رَاهْ مْشَا|rāh msha}} “(look,) he's gone”. Written short it is {{رَا|ra}}: {{رَا كْتْبْتْ لِيكْ|ra ktəbt līk}} “I did write to you”.

**{{يَاكْ|yāk}}** asks for a yes: “right?, isn't it?”: {{يَاكْ لَابَاسْ؟|yāk lābās?}} “everything's fine, isn't it?” **{{وَاخَّا|wākhkha}}** is “OK, all right”, and before a sentence “even if”: {{وَاخَّا مْعَطّْلْ، غَادِي نْجِي|wākhkha mʿaṭṭəl, ghādi nji}} “even if it's late, I'll come”.

ex.t: رَاهْ مَا كَايْنْ حْتَّى وَاحْدْ فْالدَّارْ.
ex.r: rāh ma kāyn ḥtta wāḥəd f-d-dār.

mistakes.why: {{رَاهْ|rāh}} takes the person as an ending: “I” is {{رَانِي|rāni}}.
“Isn't it?” is {{يَاكْ|yāk}}; {{وَاخَّا|wākhkha}} is “OK”.

practice.q: What does {{يَاكْ|yāk}} add to a sentence?
practice.why: {{يَاكْ|yāk}} asks the other person to agree.

practice.q: How do you say “She's just arrived”?
Your turn: a friend calls and asks where you are. Answer with {{رَانِي|rāni}}.

answers.t: رَانِي فْالدَّارْ، وَاشْ بْغِيتِي شِي حَاجَة؟
answers.r: rāni f-d-dār, wāsh bghīti shi ḥāja?
answers.tr: I'm at home, do you want something?
I'm on the bus, I'll be there soon.

lessons.title: Count: the Moroccan numbers
lessons.summary: jūj “two”, the numbers with d “of” before a noun, 11 to 19 in -ṭāsh, and prices in dirhams.
lessons.topic: {{وَاحْدْ جُوجْ تْلَاتَة…|wāḥəd jūj tlāta…}} + {{دْ|d}} + plural, {{حْضَاشْ طْنَاشْ…|ḥḍāsh ṭnāsh…}}, {{دْرْهَمْ|dərhəm}}

goal.tr: Give me two kilos of tomatoes.

blocks.p: The numbers are the Standard ones said the Darija way, with **jūj for “two”** and no case endings. Before a noun, a number from 3 to 10 is usually followed by {{دْ|d}} (“of”) and the plural with its article: {{تْلَاتَة دْ الدّْرَارِي|tlāta d d-drāri}} “three children”. A few counting words come straight after a short number: {{خْمْسْ دْقَايْقْ|khəms dqāyəq}} “five minutes”, {{عْشْرْ سْنِينْ|ʿshər snīn}} “ten years”.

**From 11 on**, the noun comes straight after the number, in the singular, as in Standard: {{طْنَاشْ سَاعَة|ṭnāsh sāʿa}} “twelve hours”, {{عْشْرِينْ دْرْهَمْ|ʿəshrīn dərhəm}} “twenty dirhams”. From 21 on, the ones come first with {{وْ|u}} “and”: {{وَاحْدْ وْ عْشْرِينْ|wāḥəd u ʿəshrīn}} “21”. **Money** is in {{دْرْهَمْ|dərhəm}} (plural {{دْرَاهْمْ|drāhəm}}); in the market many people still count in {{رْيَالْ|ryāl}}, twenty to the dirham: {{مْيَةْ رْيَالْ|myat ryāl}} is five dirhams.

ex.tr: How much is this? Fifteen dirhams.
I work twelve hours a day.

mistakes.why: A number before a noun takes {{دْ|d}} and the plural with its article.
11 to 19 end in {{ـطَاشْ|-ṭāsh}}: {{طْنَاشْ|ṭnāsh}}.

practice.q: At the market: choose your replies.

lines.why: {{هَاكْ|hāk}} “here you are” as you hand over the money.

practice.q: Your turn: say how old you are and how many people live in your house.

answers.t: عَنْدِي تْلَاتِينْ عَامْ، وْ كَنْسْكْنُو رْبْعَة فْالدَّارْ.
answers.r: ʿəndi tlātīn ʿām, u kanskənu rəbʿa f-d-dār.
answers.tr: I'm thirty, and there are four of us at home.
I'm twenty-five.

lessons.title: Say if and when: īla, kūn, mlli
lessons.summary: īla for a real “if”, kūn for “if it had been”, mlli and fāsh for “when”, ḥtta for “until”.

goal.tr: If you come early, we'll go to the beach.

blocks.p: **A real “if”** is {{إِيلَا|īla}} (also written {{إِلَا|ila}}), usually with the **past** even for the future, as in Standard after {{إِذَا|idhā}}: {{إِيلَا بْغِيتِي|īla bghīti}} “if you want”, {{إِيلَا شْفْتِيهْ، عَيّْطْ لِيَّا|īla shəftīh, ʿayyəṭ liyya}} “if you see him, call me”.

**“If it had been” (it wasn't)** is {{كُونْ|kūn}}, often twice, once in each half: {{كُونْ كْنْتْ عَارْفْ، كُونْ مَا جِيتْشْ|kūn kunt ʿārəf, kūn ma jītsh}} “if I had known, I wouldn't have come”. {{كُونْ|kūn}} with {{غِيرْ|ghīr}} is a wish: {{كُونْ غِيرْ جِيتِي!|kūn ghīr jīti!}} “if only you had come!”

**When**: {{مْلِّي|mlli}} “when, since” for what happened or happens ({{مْلِّي كْنْتْ صْغِيرْ|mlli kunt ṣghīr}} “when I was little”), {{فَاشْ|fāsh}} “when” in general, {{فُوقَاشْ|fūqāsh}} only in questions. **Until** is {{حْتَّى|ḥtta}}, **before** {{قْبَلْ مَا|qbəl ma}}, **after** {{مْنْ بْعْدْ مَا|mən baʿd ma}}, each with a verb.

ex.t: إِيلَا مَا لْقِيتِيشْ الطُّوبِيسْ، خُودْ طَاكْسِي.
ex.r: īla ma lqītīsh ṭ-ṭūbīs, khūd ṭāksi.
ex.tr: If you can't find the bus, take a taxi.

ex.t: كُونْ كَانْ عَنْدِي الْوَقْتْ، كُونْ جِيتْ.
ex.r: kūn kān ʿəndi l-waqt, kūn jīt.
ex.tr: If I'd had the time, I would have come.
When I arrived, he was asleep.
Wait for me until I come.
Wash your hands before you eat.

mistakes.why: After {{إِيلَا|īla}}, the past, even for the future.

mistakes.right: كُونْ كْنْتْ عَارْفْ، كُونْ مَا جِيتْشْ.
mistakes.rr: kūn kunt ʿārəf, kūn ma jītsh.
mistakes.tr: If I had known, I wouldn't have come.
mistakes.why: Something that didn't happen takes {{كُونْ|kūn}}, in both halves.

practice.tr: If you want, we'll go with you.

practice.q: “If I'd had the money, I would have bought it.” Which “if”?

practice.tr: When I arrived, he was asleep.
practice.why: “When” in a statement about the past: {{مْلِّي|mlli}}; {{فُوقَاشْ|fūqāsh}} is only for questions.

practice.tr: Wait for me until I come.

practice.q: How do you say “If you see him, call me”?
Your turn: say what you'll do if it rains tomorrow, and what you would have done yesterday if you'd had time.

answers.t: إِيلَا شْتَاتْ غْدَّا، غَادِي نْبْقَى فْالدَّارْ.
answers.r: īla shtāt ghədda, ghādi nbqa f-d-dār.
answers.tr: If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay at home.

answers.t: كُونْ كَانْ عَنْدِي الْوَقْتْ، كُونْ مْشِيتْ لْلسِّينِمَا.
answers.r: kūn kān ʿəndi l-waqt, kūn mshīt l-s-sinima.
answers.tr: If I'd had the time, I would have gone to the cinema.

lessons.title: Connect your ideas: lli, blli, ḥīt, bāsh
lessons.summary: lli “who, which, that” for everyone, blli “that” after say and know, ḥīt “because”, bāsh “so that”, wəlla “or”.

goal.t: قَالْ لِيَّا بْلِّي مَا غَادِيشْ يْجِي حِيتْ مْرِيضْ.
goal.r: qāl liyya blli ma ghādīsh yji ḥīt mrīḍ.
goal.tr: He told me he isn't coming because he's ill.

blocks.p: **{{اللِّي|lli}}** is the one word for “who, which, that”, for a man, a woman or many: {{الرَّاجْلْ اللِّي جَا|r-rājəl lli ja}} “the man who came”, {{الْبْنَاتْ اللِّي شْفْتْ|l-bnāt lli shəft}} “the girls I saw”. It also means “the one who, whoever”: {{اللِّي بْغَا يْجِي يْجِي|lli bgha yji yji}} “whoever wants to come can come”.

**{{بْلِّي|blli}}** is “that” after verbs of saying, knowing and thinking: {{عْرْفْتْ بْلِّي|ʿrəft blli}} “I knew that”, {{قَالْ بْلِّي|qāl blli}} “he said that”. **Because** is {{حِيتْ|ḥīt}} or {{حِيتَاشْ|ḥītāsh}}; **so that** is {{بَاشْ|bāsh}} + the bare present; **but** is {{وَلَكِنْ|walakin}}, **or** {{وْلَّا|wəlla}} (in questions too: {{أَتَايْ وْلَّا قَهْوَة؟|atāy wəlla qahwa?}} “tea or coffee?”).

table: {{الْكْتَابْ اللِّي قْرِيتْ|l-ktāb lli qrīt}} the book I read
{{عْرْفْتْ بْلِّي جَا|ʿrəft blli ja}} I knew he'd come
{{مَا جِيتْشْ حِيتْ مْرِيضْ|ma jītsh ḥīt mrīḍ}} I didn't come because I'm ill
{{جِيتْ بَاشْ نْشُوفْكْ|jīt bāsh nshūfək}} I came to see you
{{دَابَا وْلَّا غْدَّا؟|dāba wəlla ghədda?}} now or tomorrow?

ex.tr: This is the place I told you about.

ex.t: مَا كْنْتْشْ عَارْفْ بْلِّي نْتَا مْغْرْبِي.
ex.r: ma kuntsh ʿārəf blli nta məghribi.
ex.tr: I didn't know you were Moroccan.
I hurried because I was late.

ex.t: كَنْقْرَا الدَّارِجَة بَاشْ نْهْضَرْ مْعَا النَّاسْ.
ex.r: kanqra d-dārija bāsh nhḍər mʿa n-nās.
ex.tr: I'm learning Darija so I can talk to people.
Would you like tea or coffee?

mistakes.why: {{اللِّي|lli}} is the only “who, which” in Darija, for everyone.
After “say, know”, “that” is {{بْلِّي|blli}}.

practice.tr: The man who came is my brother.
I knew he was going to come.
Would you like tea or coffee?

practice.q: How do you say “I hurried because I was late”?
Your turn: say why you are learning Darija, with {{حِيتْ|ḥīt}} or {{بَاشْ|bāsh}}.

answers.tr: I'm learning Darija because my wife is Moroccan.

answers.t: بَاشْ نْفْهَمْ النَّاسْ مْلِّي نْمْشِي لْلْمْغْرِبْ.
answers.r: bāsh nfham n-nās mlli nmshi l-l-məghrib.
answers.tr: So I can understand people when I go to Morocco.
